metadata.title: Can teacher support reduce inequalities in education? Re-examining the relationship between cultural
metadata.venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 student microdata for reading performance and questionnaire-based indices (cultural capital and teacher support). The manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling weights (and any replicate weights) were applied in the regression/moderation analyses, so the weighting strategy is unclear. Because PISA employs a complex multistage sampling design with clustering at school and country levels, analysts should use the official PISA student/sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) when estimating uncertainty. The paper also does not describe any additional preprocessing tied to weights (e.g., weight trimming), so readers should treat the reported significance tests as conditional on the authors’ (unstated) weighting/variance approach.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe how missing questionnaire responses or any missingness in the constructed indices (cultural capital and teacher support) were handled, nor does it report an imputation or deletion rule. This is a reporting gap because PISA questionnaire items typically have non-trivial missingness, and the moderation results depend on the composite indices derived from multiple Likert items and home resources.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The authors first compute the correlation between cultural capital and PISA 2018 reading performance for all OECD countries (37 countries; 294,527 students). They then rank countries by the correlation coefficient and select two comparative groups of six countries total: (i) Hungary, France, and the Czech Republic (strongest correlations) and (ii) Israel, Canada, and Norway (weakest correlations). The moderation analyses are performed separately for these two country groups using students’ PISA 2018 reading scores and constructed indices for cultural capital (from parents’ education and home resources) and teacher support (from seven Likert items).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (OECD countries with strongest cultural capital–reading correlation; grades not specified)
main_findings.target_variable: Reading performance (moderation: cultural capital × teacher support)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical multiple regression: Step 1 R² = 0.184, F(2, 16418) = 1854.92, p < .001; interaction ΔR² = 0.001, ΔF(3, 16417) = 14.532, p < .001; interaction coefficient b = 3.81, t(16417) = 3.81, p < .01. Correlation is enhanced: teacher support increases the cultural capital–reading correlation; cultural capital effect stronger at high teacher support (low: 16th percentile; average: 50th; high: 86th).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading the study leveraged Cultural capital index and Teacher support index (within the education systems with the strongest cultural capital–reading correlation) to predict Reading performance, finding that the cultural capital–reading relationship is moderated by teacher support with a small but significant interaction (ΔR² = 0.001, p < .001) and an enhancing pattern. This indicates that strengthening teacher support may amplify the cultural capital gradient in more stratified systems, so equity-oriented teacher support policies should be designed to avoid widening gaps.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (OECD countries with weakest cultural capital–reading correlation; grades not specified)
main_findings.target_variable: Reading performance (moderation: cultural capital × teacher support)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical multiple regression: Step 1 R² = 0.052, F(2, 29195) = 795.6, p < .001; interaction ΔR² = 0.0002, ΔF(3, 29194) = 7.478, p = .006; interaction coefficient b = −1.5368, t(29194) = −2.7346, p = .006. Interaction pattern: teacher support decreases the cultural capital–reading correlation; cultural capital effect stronger at low teacher support than high teacher support; low cultural capital benefits most from high teacher support.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading the study leveraged Cultural capital index and Teacher support index (within the education systems with the weakest cultural capital–reading correlation) to predict Reading performance, finding that the cultural capital–reading relationship is moderated by teacher support with a significant negative interaction (ΔR² = 0.0002, p = .006). This indicates that teacher support can help reduce inequality by disproportionately benefiting students with low cultural capital in more equitable systems, though the study’s cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 student data to examine whether teacher support moderates the association between a constructed cultural capital index and reading performance, and whether this moderation differs across education systems. Countries were first ranked by the cultural capital–reading correlation across 37 OECD countries (294,527 students), then six countries were grouped into “strongest” (Hungary, France, Czech Republic) and “weakest” (Israel, Canada, Norway) correlation sets for separate moderation analyses. The authors report hierarchical multiple regression results: in the strongest-correlation group, Step 1 R² = 0.184 and the interaction adds ΔR² = 0.001 (p < .001), with an enhancing pattern; in the weakest-correlation group, Step 1 R² = 0.052 and the interaction adds ΔR² = 0.0002 (p = .006), with a decreasing pattern. No machine-learning models are evaluated (the analysis is moderation via regression), and the paper does not report missing-data handling or whether PISA sampling weights were applied, limiting interpretability for policy inference.
